results.answer: A segment tree has only O(log n) levels, and a range query visits at most a constant number of nodes per level, so the total number of visited nodes is O(log n). Thus the query climbs the tree level‑by‑level and finishes in O(log n) time【2】【5】.

The union‑find structure determines if two elements are in the same set by using the find operation to obtain each element’s representative and then comparing those representatives; if the representatives are equal, the elements belong to the same set【4】【5】.

The Z‑algorithm builds the Z‑array in a single left‑to‑right scan, keeping a window [x, y] that is the rightmost segment of the string that matches its prefix. For each position k it first looks at the previously computed value z[k‑x]; if k + z[k‑x] < y it can copy that value (z[k] = z[k‑x]), otherwise it must compare characters one by one starting at y‑k+1 and y+1 to extend the match and update the window [x, y] as needed [4][3]. This use of the stored Z‑values and the [x, y] range lets the whole array be constructed in O(n) time.

A topological sort yields a linear ordering of all the vertices of a directed acyclic graph such that whenever there is a path from node a to node b, node a appears earlier than node b in the order. [1]

Yes. By building a prefix‑sum (or difference) array in advance you can answer any interval‑sum query in O(1): the sum of a stretch [a,b] is just prefix[b] − prefix[a‑1] (or the corresponding difference‑array lookup). [5]

Jumping to the middle (binary search) repeatedly halves the portion of the list that still needs to be examined, so the region size shrinks exponentially and the search runs in O(log n) time. Walking through the list checks elements one by one, requiring up to n comparisons and thus O(n) time, which is slower for large n [4].

Compute a hash (fingerprint) for each piece of text and compare the hash values; if the hashes are equal the texts are considered identical, though a collision (different texts with the same hash) is possible if the hash constants are poorly chosen. [1]

To obtain the two nodes that are farthest apart (the tree’s diameter), compute for each node the maximum length of a path that starts at that node; the largest of these lengths is the diameter, and its endpoints are the desired points. This can be done in linear time O(n) by a depth‑first or breadth‑first search that first finds a farthest node from an arbitrary start, then finds the farthest node from that one — the resulting pair are the endpoints of the longest path [4].

Keep a monotonic queue (deque) of candidates for the minimum. When the window moves, discard elements from the back that are larger than the new element, add the new element to the back, and remove the front element if it has slid out of the window; the element at the front is always the current minimum [1][5].

Because the total work can be bounded by a constant amount per element: each element is added to the stack once and removed at most once, so even if a removal sometimes requires many steps, the overall number of stack operations is at most 2 per element, giving a total of O(n) work and an average (amortized) cost of O(1) per operation【4】.

Picking the largest‑value coin first can be suboptimal for non‑canonical coin systems; for example, with coins {1, 3, 4} and target 6 the greedy method yields 4 + 1 + 1 while the optimal solution is 3 + 3【1】.  
The failure is avoided by solving the coin‑change problem with dynamic programming, which computes the minimum‑coin count for any set of denominations【5】.

Beyond simple range‑sum queries, a segment tree can be built to answer many other range queries such as minimum and maximum queries, greatest‑common‑divisor queries, and bit‑wise operations like AND, OR and XOR【1】【3】.

Both data structures answer range queries in O(log n) time, but a binary indexed tree (BIT) is limited to sum queries while a segment tree can handle many other queries such as minimum, maximum, or frequency counts [5][1]. A BIT is simpler and uses less memory, whereas a segment tree requires more memory and is harder to implement but is far more general [1]. Choose a BIT when you only need fast range‑sum updates; pick a segment tree when you need other types of range queries or more flexibility.
